title: 99 Million People Live with Multiple Chronic Conditions
summary: 99 million insured adults have multiple chronic conditions. Thomas Tsang, MD, on where fragmented care fails and what employers should ask care partners.
body_markdown:
November 12, 2026


# 99 Million People Live with Multiple Chronic Conditions


By


[Thomas Tsang, MD, MPH](https://www.linkedin.com/in/thomas-tsang-md-mph-08b5494)


This edition covers:


- What managing more than one chronic condition looks like for patients


- Where care for multiple conditions breaks down


- What benefits leaders and medical directors should ask of their care partners now


When I worked in-clinic, I saw 25 to 30 patients per day, about 10 mins per visit. Most of my patients came in to manage not just a single condition, but several conditions at the same time. They were predominantly cardiovascular and cardiometabolic diseases like high cholesterol and diabetes.


While the four, 10-minute doctor appointments over a calendar year were vital to each patient’s care plan, they weren’t enough to support them in the time between visits when lifestyle choices were being made.


Consider a patient I'll call Maria. She is 54, works full time, and has type 2 diabetes and high cholesterol.


Her primary care physician (PCP) prescribes both of her medications and sees her twice a year. Metformin, the usual first-line diabetes medication, keeps her


[A1C](https://diabetes.org/about-diabetes/a1c)


near goal. Atorvastatin, a statin, lowers her low-density lipoprotein (LDL) or "bad," cholesterol by reducing how much the liver makes.


Maria also wants to lose 15 pounds, but doesn’t have time to bring it up in her short visit with her PCP. She sees ads online for GLP-1 medications promising quick weight loss. After a brief intake questionnaire, she starts a compounded GLP-1 through a cash-pay online subscription, unaware that she could get it covered for her diabetes. The online prescriber never asks for her labs, and Maria doesn't mention the new medication to her PCP.


Maria is now managing three different medications, each with their own set of side effects and recommended lifestyle changes.


Within weeks, the three care paths start to collide. She has decided on her own to start a keto diet to manage her diabetes with a goal of getting off the metformin. Meanwhile, high-fat meals are a


[common trigger for nausea,](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12992036/)


which is often exacerbated by GLP-1 medications. She sees online that GLP-1s can cause nausea, so she stops the GLP-1 and keeps the keto diet. Meanwhile, keto is working against the statin she takes for her high cholesterol. In this scenario, there’s limited progress being made on her overall health.


## The Scale of the Problem


In 2023, 51.4% of U.S. adults


roughly 131 million people, reported two or more chronic conditions,


[according to CDC data.](https://www.cdc.gov/pcd/issues/2025/24_0539.htm#:~:text=Moreover,%2051.4%%20(representing%20130%20million)%20of%20US%20adults%20reported%20MCC,)


By Omada's analysis,


[99 million insured adults live with two or more](https://stockanalysis.com/stocks/omda/transcripts/710606-investor-day-2026/)


of the chronic conditions


[we treat.](https://www.omadahealth.com/for-organizations#)


Among U.S. adults diagnosed with diabetes, the


[CDC's National Diabetes Statistics Report](https://usdss.cdc.gov/diabetes/report.html)


found 88% had overweight or obesity and 38% had elevated cholesterol. Our own member data look the same:


[70% to 80% of members](https://www.omadahealth.com/resource-center/7-healthcare-industry-myths-omada-insights-vs-industry-beliefs)


in Omada's diabetes and hypertension programs have multiple conditions.


Mental health belongs in that cluster as well. People with conditions like


[cardiovascular disease](https://www.heart.org/en/news/2020/11/20/people-with-depression-fare-worse-in-heart-health-study#:~:text=In%20fact,%20research%20suggests%2015%%20to%2030%%20of%20people%20with%20cardiovascular%20disease%20have%20depression%20%E2%80%93%20a%20rate%20two%20to%20three%20times%20higher%20than%20the%20general%20population.)


and


[diabetes](https://www.cdc.gov/diabetes/living-with/mental-health.html#:~:text=People%20with%20diabetes%20are%202%20to%203%20times%20more%20likely%20to%20have%20depression%20than%20people%20without%20diabetes.)


are more likely to experience depression. Depression can impact how a person


[eats, sleeps, moves](https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/depression/symptoms-causes/syc-20356007)


and


[takes medication](https://www.ama-assn.org/practice-management/ama-steps-forward-program/8-reasons-patients-dont-take-their-medications#:~:text=Patients%20who%20are%20depressed%20are%20less%20likely%20to%20take%20their%20medications%20as%20prescribed.)


. It can shape whether patients like Maria seek care when feeling sick or quietly decide to stop taking important medications.


## Multiple Conditions, Fragmented Care


Maria has two prescribers who don't know about each other, and no one guiding the daily decisions that drive her overall care.


A 2026 analysis by the American Diabetes Association found that among U.S. adults with diabetes who see multiple providers, one in four had


[unmet care coordination needs](https://diabetesjournals.org/diabetes/article/75/Supplement_1/2000-P/168206/2000-P-Unmet-Care-Coordination-Needs-in-Primary)


. More than half of U.S. adults now have


[records in multiple patient portals](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK616185/)


, and Americans spend the


[equivalent of an eight-hour workday each month](https://www.aapa.org/news-central/2023/05/u-s-adults-spend-eight-hours-monthly-coordinating-healthcare-find-system-overwhelming/)


coordinating care.


That burden shows up in outcomes.


Among Medicare patients with three or four chronic conditions, those with the most fragmented care were 14% more likely to visit the emergency department than those with the least. A national cohort linked highly fragmented care to an 18% higher risk of hospitalization in the following three months.


#### Why Single-Point Care Solutions Don’t Work


Benefits strategies overwhelmingly buy care by condition: a diabetes solution, a hypertension platform, a weight or GLP-1 program, for example. Each reports its own outcomes.


Those reports have value, but each program measures the condition it was built for, not the patient’s entire cardiometabolic picture.


Single-solution programs raise the risk of conflicting care. A diabetes program likely coaches toward the carb cuts that move A1C. A cholesterol program pushes the fiber and saturated-fat guidance that moves LDL.


While a very low-carb, high-fat diet can do wonders for A1C levels, it can also


[raise LDL cholesterol](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13281555/)


. When Maria’s next lipid panel comes back higher, her PCP may not know her diet had changed; they haven’t had the time to discuss how Maria is managing her health in the time between visits, so they raise her statin dose with intentions of protecting her heart. That treats the side effect of one dietary element, not the root of the issue.


Conflicting care doesn't improve health over time. Managing one condition well while the others drift is how cumulative cardiometabolic burden builds.


Multi-condition care treats the person as a single outcome. For Maria, that means discussing all medications and dietary changes with her PCP first, giving her the opportunity to weigh her options. If Maria still chooses to do keto, her provider now knows to keep a closer eye on her labs to see if any medications need to be adjusted.


## What to Ask For Now


Questions for employers and health plans to ask every care partner in 2027:


- Who has visibility of the full medication list for a member with multiple conditions, including prescriptions from outside their PCP?


- When treatment changes for one condition, who adjusts the rest of the care plan?


- Is distress screened for and acted on inside the same care plan?


- Are outcomes reported per person across conditions, or per program?


If the answers point to separate vendors and care paths for overlapping conditions, the 99 million will only increase.
